Triangular J1J_{1}-J2J_{2} Heisenberg Antiferromagnet in a Magnetic Field

T. Abstract

The behavior of the paradigmatic J1−J2J_{1}-J_{2} triangular lattice Heisenberg antiferromagnet in a magnetic field remains unsettled despite decades of study. We map out the phase diagram using three complementary approaches, including self-consistent nonlinear spin-wave theory, density-matrix renormalization group, and variational Monte Carlo. This combined analysis resolves the competition among different field-induced magnetic orders and magnetization plateaux across the classically frustrated parameter range. In particular, there is a finite range in the parameter regime around J2/J1=18J_{2}/J_{1}=\frac{1}{8} in which i) upon the application of the external field, the gapless quantum spin liquid acquires a finite density of monopoles, and ii) by further increasing the field, two plateaux are clearly obtained at m=13m=\frac{1}{3} and m=12m=\frac{1}{2}. We discuss the experimental importance of the consecutive magnetization plateaux transitions as a signature of an underlying quantum spin-liquid phase.

Introduction– Triangular lattice antiferromagnets (TrAFM) are not only widely-used illustrations of geometrically frustrated magnets, but arguably the founding examples of an entire research field [26]. Famously, Wannier showed that the triangular Ising model realizes a critical liquid with an extensive classical ground state degeneracy [45] and the frustration is also manifest as an unusual step-like magnetization process of the model as a function of an applied magnetic field. Early on, it was shown that the magnetization jumps from zero to a plateau value m=13m=\frac{1}{3} and then to full saturation [27]. Adding further next-nearest-neighbor (NNN) interactions J2J_{2} in addition to the standard nearest-neighbor (NN) J1J_{1} one enables a new magnetization plateau at m=12m=\frac{1}{2} [28, 6] from the interplay between geometric and exchange frustration. Beyond Ising models, the phase diagram is even richer for triangular Heisenberg-like systems with quantum fluctuations [29, 10] and thermal fluctuations stabilizing collinear plateaux phases [23, 15, 36]. In general, the study of magnetization plateaus has a long history [43, 42, 17] and is a telltale experimental signature of magnetic frustration [30, 40].

The interest in the TrAFM has significantly increased in recent years because their competing interactions can stabilize sought-after quantum spin liquids (QSLs) [32, 25, 7] in a number of candidate materials [22, 52, 14, 51, 12, 34, 39]. Since Anderson’s original proposal [3], the S=12S=\frac{1}{2} Heisenberg TrAFM has been a prominent theoretical candidate for realizing a QSL ground state. Indeed, upon the addition of NNN Heisenberg exchange of strength 0.07≲J2/J1≲0.160.07\lesssim J_{2}/J_{1}\lesssim 0.16 a QSL is by now well established numerically [18, 20, 13, 44]. Recent progress on the experimental side has suggested that the Yb-based delafossites are expected to be accurately modeled by this type of Heisenberg model [33, 47, 34] but finding unambiguous signatures of QSL behavior remains a challenge [25, 35]. In this context, studying the phase diagram of TrAFM models beyond the QSL regime is important to gain theoretical insights into their stability and the degree to which basic models resemble physical materials.

In this work we study the phase diagram of the spin-12\frac{1}{2} Heisenberg TrAFM in a magnetic field described by the Hamiltonian

ℋ=J1​∑⟨i​j⟩S→i⋅S→j+J2​∑⟨⟨i​j⟩⟩S→i⋅S→j−H​∑iSiz\mathcal{H}=J_{1}\sum_{\langle ij\rangle}\vec{S}_{i}\cdot\vec{S}_{j}+J_{2}\sum_{\langle\langle ij\rangle\rangle}\vec{S}_{i}\cdot\vec{S}_{j}-H\sum_{i}S_{i}^{z} (1)

and concentrate on 0≤J2/J1≤10\leq J_{2}/J_{1}\leq 1. The classical limit exhibits a three-sublattice phase for 0≤J2/J1≤180\leq J_{2}/J_{1}\leq\frac{1}{8}, a four-sublattice phase for 18≤J2/J1≤1\frac{1}{8}\leq J_{2}/J_{1}\leq 1 and a fully polarized phase for H≥max⁡{4.5​J1,4​(J1+J2)}H\geq\max\{4.5J_{1},4(J_{1}+J_{2})\}, yet the ground state is infinitely degenerate in the former two (see supplemental material [1]). Quantum fluctuations lift the degeneracy, which has been extensively studied and verified in the zero field limit [21, 9, 19]. Furthermore, the phase diagram for small and large J2J_{2} including a magnetic field has been studied in linear spin wave theory (LSWT) with self-consistent non-linear spin wave theory (NLSWT) applied to the plateaux and Ginzburg-Landau theory on condensates [11, 50, 49].

Despite the long research history, several open questions remain: i) the precise location of phase boundaries; ii) the extent of the magnetization plateaux around the interesting classical frustration point J2/J1=18J_{2}/J_{1}=\frac{1}{8}; iii) the validity of semiclassical approaches; and, most importantly, iv) the fate of the critical QSL when switching on a magnetic field. Here, we determine the phase diagram by combining NLSWT, density-matrix renormalization group (DMRG) [46, 16], and variational Monte Carlo (VMC) [4] analyses. Within NLSWT, we implement the Holstein–Primakoff (HP) transformation and extract self-consistent solutions including quantum corrections up to second order (S−2S^{-2}) across the full range of J2J_{2} and HH under study. We place these results alongside independent DMRG and VMC calculations on representative cuts through the phase space, using these complementary approaches to cross-validate one another and thereby establish the phase diagram shown in Fig. 1. Remarkably, we find overlapping m=13m=\frac{1}{3} and m=12m=\frac{1}{2} magnetization plateaux above the zero-field QSL regime. Thus, the experimental observation of such consecutive plateaux is a strong indication that the Hamiltonian is in a parameter regime allowing for a zero field QSL. In addition, we show that applying a field to the critical QSL leads to a ground state with a finite density of monopoles; see Fig. 1 for a quantitative estimate of the phase diagram in vicinity of the QSL regime.

Semiclassical Theory.– We begin by outlining details of the well known HP transformation to obtain quantum corrections to classical ground states. The states considered are not collinear, hence the transformation is applied in a rotated frame S→′\vec{S}^{\prime}, chosen such that the zz-axis is aligned with the respective classical spin direction. The spin inside the Hamiltonian is obtained using a standard rotation matrix RR such that S→=R​S→′\vec{S}=R\vec{S}^{\prime}. The transformation itself is given as

S′⁣+=2​S−a†​a​a,S′z=S−a†​a,S^{\prime+}=\sqrt{2S-a^{\dagger}a}a,~~S^{\prime z}=S-a^{\dagger}a, (2)

which we then expand for large SS.

To compute the ground state energy, we include up to quartic terms in the expansion of the full Hamiltonian, and treat quartic and cubic terms self-consistently. Since the ground state is (not always) collinear, we need to additionally consider terms linear in the operators. For classical ground states, the leading order vanishes; however, higher orders require a renormalization of angles such that any term linear in the bosonic creation and annihilation operators vanishes. For this work, we need the renormalized set of angles θ\theta up to order S−1S^{-1}, which is generally determined from the requirement

ℋ(1)​(θ)+1S​ℋ¯(3)​(θ)=0+𝒪⁡(S−2),\mathcal{H}^{(1)}(\theta)+\frac{1}{S}\overline{\mathcal{H}}^{(3)}(\theta)=0+\mathcal{O}(S^{-2}), (3)

combined with preserving the classical limit θ=θcl+𝒪⁡(S−1)\theta=\theta_{\text{cl}}+\mathcal{O}(S^{-1}). The overline (ℋ¯\overline{\mathcal{H}}) indicates that terms have been contracted to scalar, linear and quadratic order in the boson operators. Solving this equation for θ\theta yields the proper set of renormalized angles. We use the angle determined from these equations inside the Hamiltonian and perform the expansion thereof. In doing so, we do not expand the angle in S−1S^{-1} but rather treat it akin to a variational parameter

ℋ⁡(θ)=ℋcl​(θ)+1S​ℋ(2)​(θ)+1S2​ℋ¯(4)​(θ)=N​Ecl​(θ)+12​S​∑𝐤(a𝐤†​M𝐤​(θ)​a𝐤−Δ𝐤),\begin{split}\mathcal{H}(\theta)&=\mathcal{H}_{\text{cl}}(\theta)+\frac{1}{S}\mathcal{H}^{(2)}(\theta)+\frac{1}{S^{2}}\overline{\mathcal{H}}^{(4)}(\theta)\\ &=NE_{\text{cl}}(\theta)+\frac{1}{2S}\sum_{\mathbf{k}}\left(a_{\mathbf{k}}^{\dagger}M_{\mathbf{k}}(\theta)a_{\mathbf{k}}-\Delta_{\mathbf{k}}\right),\end{split} (4)

where NN is the total number of lattice sites and the sum runs over all accessible points in the Brillouin zone. The ground state (GS) energy is then obtained by diagonalizing the Hamiltonian under periodic boundary conditions (PBC) using a standard Bogoliubov transformation.

To obtain a self-consistent solution, we make use of complementary two algorithms: The local algorithm works at a single point in parameter space. At every step, it uses a linear combination of mean-field parameters from the previous two steps at some mixing angle and computes the ground state energy from Eq. (4) and new mean-field parameters from the eigenvalues thereof. This process is repeated until the energy has converged within bounds of 10−910^{-9} for ten consecutive steps. Since this algorithm is prone to runaway effects and lattice-size-dependent instabilities, we use the stable algorithm as a cross check. In this case, the local algorithm is performed at a point J2(0)J_{2}^{(0)}, H(0)H^{(0)} in parameter space, for which the ground state is well defined. The mean-field parameters of this solution are then used analogous to the local algorithm, however additionally modifying the parameters J2J_{2} and HH in small increments at every step. Clearly, the stable algorithm is preferable for computing the phase diagram (in the sense of computational cost) if the state is stable and adiabatically connected to the previous state. In contrast, the local algorithm is able to capture self-consistent ground states that may not be adiabatically connected to neighboring states in the sense of the MF parameters.

Phase Diagram and Magnetization Plateaux.– The semiclassical analysis outlined above predicts the rich phase structure shown in the top panel of Fig. 1. At H=0H=0, LSWT predicts a breakdown of the Y state, and hence any 120∘ ordered state, at J2/J1≳0.085J_{2}/J_{1}\gtrsim 0.085 while the Stripe phase has no self-consistent solution without condensates below J2/J1≲0.16J_{2}/J_{1}\lesssim 0.16, in agreement with the current literature. We thus find a finite region in parameter space connected to the QSL regime in which none of the classical states investigated are stable, as denoted by the purple box in the top panel of Fig. 1. The low-field phase diagram near the QMC regime is instead given by the VMC approach shown in the bottom panel of Fig. 1, whose details are to be discussed in the next section. Note, contrary to previous works [50, 49], we find that the stripe state is not the ground state close to the fully polarized phase for J2/J1≥18J_{2}/J_{1}\geq\frac{1}{8} in self-consistent NLSWT. We also verified that the umbrella state, defined as an in-plane 120∘120^{\circ} order with all spins canted along the direction of the magnetic field, is never the self-consistent solution in the phase diagram with lowest energy within our NLSWT.

We now obtain a complete semiclassical characterization of the magnetic phases for H≠0H\neq 0 and variable next-nearest-neighbor exchange. In addition to the well-known field-induced UUD phase at small J2J_{2}, we find two consecutive magnetization plateaux at distinct magnetic fields: the UUD plateau with m=13m=\frac{1}{3} for small-to-moderate NNN exchange 0<J2/J1≲140<J_{2}/J_{1}\lesssim\frac{1}{4} at moderate fields (blue area in Fig. 2a), and the UUUD plateau with m=12m=\frac{1}{2} for J2/J1≳0.08J_{2}/J_{1}\gtrsim 0.08 at slightly higher fields (green area in Fig. 2b). Both plateaux remain stable beyond the classical regime in HH and J2J_{2} once non-linear corrections are included. Remarkably, as clearly shown in Fig. 2b, there is an overlapping window around J2/J1∼18J_{2}/J_{1}\sim\frac{1}{8} in which both UUD and UUUD phases appear successively upon increasing the field, while a QSL is expected in the zero-field limit. This two-plateau structure therefore provides a useful diagnostic of the range of NNN Heisenberg couplings where a Dirac QSL is likely to occur at low fields, albeit its robustness against anisotropies remains an open question for future work.

The consecutive magnetization plateaux could be accessible experimentally not only through chemical tuning of the exchange ratio but also via application of pressure or strain. Similar tuning has been achieved on Kitaev and Heisenberg interactions on the honeycomb lattice [48, 31]. In recent experiments on the TrAFM [34, 5], the m=13m=\frac{1}{3} plateau has been observed while the m=12m=\frac{1}{2} plateau was absent for candidate materials NaYbSe2 and TlYbSe2 which have J2/J1J_{2}/J_{1} ratios for which we predict the m=12m=\frac{1}{2} plateau to exist. It points to the relevance of other non-Heisenberg interactions which can destabilize the plateaux. For example, an easy-plane anisotropy of the NNN exchange interaction energetically favors the canted stripe state compared to the UUUD plateau. Such XXZ-type anisotropies have been shown to persist beyond classical approximations in the J2=0J_{2}=0 sector [38]. Single-ion easy-axis anisotropies have also been shown to impact the extent of plateaux’s [37]. Furthermore, Dzyaloshinskii-Moriya or spin-scalar-chirality type interactions may destabilize plateaus as well.

Although NLSWT offers a controlled semiclassical description of the competing ordered phases, we subject its predictions to a stricter test using unbiased DMRG. The DMRG calculations, while necessarily performed on finite cylinders and therefore subject to finite-size constraints, fully incorporate quantum fluctuations and produce magnetization curves that remain consistent with the semiclassical phase structure across all accessible system sizes. Specifically, we perform grand-canonical DMRG (i.e. without fixing the total magnetization) on a 6×246\times 24 cylinder with fixed bond dimension χ=1600\chi=1600 and controlled truncation error ∼10−7\sim 10^{-7}, thus obtaining the optimal magnetization mm for each field HH. Calculations along several cuts of the phase diagram are shown in Fig. 2. The resulting magnetization curve is then directly compared to the magnetization obtained in NLSWT:

m=1S​NUC​∑i=1NUCcos⁡(θi)⁡(S−ni)m=\frac{1}{S{N_{\text{UC}}}}\sum_{i=1}^{N_{\text{UC}}}\cos(\theta_i)(S-n_{i}) (5)

where ni=⟨ai†​ai⟩n_{i}=\expectationvalue*{a_i^\dagger a_i} and NUC{N_{\text{UC}}} are respectively the boson occupation number and the number of sites per unit cell.

Figure 2a shows the cut in HH with a fixed small J2/J1=0.005J_{2}/J_{1}=0.005, where we find quantitative agreement between both algorithms of NLSWT and DMRG simulations in all magnetic phases. For larger J2/J1=0.15J_{2}/J_{1}=0.15, shown in Fig. 2b, the same progression of phases is obtained in both methods; remarkably, both methods predict two successive magnetization plateaux (blue and green), albeit with minor deviations in the precise location of phase transition. It should be noted that these minor deviations lie close to the classical phase transition at J2/J1=18J_{2}/J_{1}=\frac{1}{8}, where we observe mean-field parameters like nin_{i} becoming larger, thus worsening the predictive power of NLSWT. This is visible in Figs. 2c and d, cuts along J2/J1J_{2}/J_{1} at fixed magnetic fields H=1.5H=1.5 and H=2.5H=2.5 respectively, where the quantitative agreement between NLSWT and DMRG breaks down close to J2/J1=18J_{2}/J_{1}=\frac{1}{8} [dotted lines in Figs. 2c, d]. Despite the perturbative nature of NLSWT and the finite-size effects of DMRG, the close agreement between these complementary methods lends strong support to the magnetic phases we identify. By contrast, in the non-magnetic QSL regime in the zero-field limit (purple box in Fig. 1), NLSWT breaks down completely.

VMC analysis in the vicinity of QSL phase– To probe the frustrated regime near J2/J1=18J_{2}/J_{1}=\frac{1}{8}, we employ a VMC approach based on Gutzwiller-projected fermionic wavefunctions representing the relevant competing orders. For each fixed SzS^{z} sector, from 00 up to m=13m=\frac{1}{3}, we construct and optimize the corresponding ansätze (e.g., canted-stripe, umbrella, Y, and monopole states) and compare their variational energies to assess the dominant correlations. The unprojected fermionic hamiltonian has the general form ℋaux=∑⟨i​j⟩,σχi​jci​σ†cj​σ+H.c.+∑iM→i⋅S→i\mathcal{H}_{\rm aux}=\sum_{\langle ij\rangle,\sigma}\chi_{ij}c_{i\sigma}^{\dagger}c_{j\sigma}+{\rm H.c.}+\sum_{i}\vec{M}_{i}\cdot\vec{S}_{i}, where the parameters χi​j\chi_{ij} and M→i\vec{M}_{i} differ for each phase (details to be provided in [2]). In particular, the monopole states (corresponding to finite densities of the gapless monopole excitations of the Dirac spin liquid [41]) have M→i=0\vec{M}_{i}=0 and are generated by threading an internal gauge flux 2​π​Q2\pi Q uniformly through all triangles [8] and occupying the resulting 2​Q2Q fermionic zero modes with up spins, yielding a unique state with Sz=QS^{z}=Q. The corresponding magnetization curve at J2/J1=18J_{2}/J_{1}=\frac{1}{8} is shown in Fig. 3. The projected monopole states, despite having no tunable parameters, maintain the lowest variational energy among all competing ansätze up to H/J1≈1.15H/J_{1}\approx 1.15 (m≈16m\approx\frac{1}{6}), beyond which a sharp first-order transition occurs into the Y phase. The VMC-based estimate of the phase boundaries is provided in the bottom panel of Fig. 1. These results demonstrate that in the vicinity of the QSL, the ground state in the presence of a field is a state with a finite density of monopoles. A detailed characterization of this phase is given in a companion work [2].

Discussion and Conclusion.– We obtained the phase diagram of the J1−J2−HJ_{1}-J_{2}-H triangular lattice Heisenberg antiferromagnet by integrating three complementary methods: self-consistent NLSWT (including all S−2S^{-2} corrections), large-scale DMRG, and variational Monte Carlo. NLSWT provides global structure and identifies candidate phases; DMRG supplies an unbiased quantum benchmark along representative cuts; VMC resolves the regime where semiclassical methods fail—namely the vicinity of the classical frustration point J2/J1=18J_{2}/J_{1}=\frac{1}{8}, where the zero-field Dirac QSL emerges. Taken together, the methods yield a coherent and internally consistent phase diagram. First, non-linear quantum fluctuations substantially enlarge both the UUD (m=13m=\frac{1}{3}) and UUUD (m=12m=\frac{1}{2}) plateaux in both HH and J2/J1J_{2}/J_{1}. Second, these plateaux overlap in the parameter window connected to the zero-field QSL: increasing the field produces two successive magnetization plateaux at m=13m=\frac{1}{3} and m=12m=\frac{1}{2}, a distinctive experimental fingerprint of a system tuned close to the QSL regime. Third, away from phase boundaries and the QSL region, NLSWT with fully renormalized angles quantitatively reproduces the DMRG results, confirming its reliability over most of the phase diagram. Finally, VMC shows that applying a field onto a Dirac QSL leads to a finite-density monopole phase that persists up to a first-order transition into the Y state. Its detailed characterization is addressed in a companion work [2].

Appendix S1 General Framework

Our goal is to compute quantum corrections and magnon dispersion around classical ground states of the J1−J2−HJ_{1}-J_{2}-H model on the triangular lattice, defined by the Hamiltonian

ℋ=J1S2​∑⟨i​j⟩S→i⋅S→j+J2S2​∑⟨⟨i​j⟩⟩S→i⋅S→j−HS​∑iSiz.\mathcal{H}=\frac{J_{1}}{S^{2}}\sum_{\langle ij\rangle}\vec{S}_{i}\cdot\vec{S}_{j}+\frac{J_{2}}{S^{2}}\sum_{\langle\langle ij\rangle\rangle}\vec{S}_{i}\cdot\vec{S}_{j}-\frac{H}{S}\sum_{i}S_{i}^{z}. (S1)

We have normalized all interactions by the spin quantum number, such that the classical phase transitions are independent of S=|S→i|S=\absolutevalue*{\vec{S}_i}.

Expanding around a classical state amounts to performing an expansion around large SS, i.e. an expansion in S−1S^{-1}. For this, we shall use the Holstein Primakoff method, where a spin, classically aligned in the positive zz-direction is expressed in terms of bosonic operators a,a†a,a^{\dagger} as

S+=2​S−a†​a​aSz=S−a†​a,\begin{split}S^{+}=&\sqrt{2S-a^{\dagger}a}a\\ S^{z}=&S-a^{\dagger}a,\end{split} (S2)

such that ⟨Si→⟩=S​e→z+𝒪⁡(S−12)\expectationvalue{\vec{S_i}}=S\vec{e}_{z}+\mathcal{O}(S^{-\frac{1}{2}}). For an arbitrarily rotated classical spin, determined by the polar and azimuthal angles θ,ϕ\theta,\phi, the expansion is performed in a rotated, local frame, such that the spin in the laboratory frame is given by

S→=Rϕ​Rθ​S→′,\vec{S}=R_{\phi}R_{\theta}\vec{S}^{\prime}, (S3)

leading to the very general expression

(SxSySz)=(cθ​cϕ​S′x−sϕ​S′y+sθ​cϕ​S′zsϕ​(S′x​cθ+S′z​sθ)+S′y​cϕS′z​cθ−S′x​sθ),\left(\begin{array}[]{c}S^{x}\\ S^{y}\\ S^{z}\end{array}\right)=\left(\begin{array}[]{c}c_{\theta}c_{\phi}{S^{\prime}}^{x}-s_{\phi}{S^{\prime}}^{y}+s_{\theta}c_{\phi}{S^{\prime}}^{z}\\ s_{\phi}({S^{\prime}}^{x}c_{\theta}+{S^{\prime}}^{z}s_{\theta})+{S^{\prime}}^{y}c_{\phi}\\ {S^{\prime}}^{z}c_{\theta}-{S^{\prime}}^{x}s_{\theta}\end{array}\right), (S4)

where we plug in the expansion from Eq. (S2) for the components S′S^{\prime}. Using an ordinary Taylor expansion, we thus obtain an expansion in S−1S^{-1} (or, more precisely, S−12S^{-\frac{1}{2}}).

Appendix S2 Classical Ground States

The classical ground states of the system are given in terms of a three- or four-site unit cell for 0≤J2≤180\leq J_{2}\leq\frac{1}{8} and 18≤J2≤1\frac{1}{8}\leq J_{2}\leq 1, respectively.

S2.1 Three-Site Unit Cell

For NUC=3{N_{\text{UC}}}=3, the classical Hamiltonian may be rewritten as

ℋcl=J1​Np4​S2[(S→1+S→2+S→3−S​H​e→z3​J1)2+6​S2​J2J1−3S2−S2​H29​J12],\begin{split}\mathcal{H}_{\text{cl}}=\frac{J_{1}N_{p}}{4S^{2}}&\left[\left(\vec{S}_{1}+\vec{S}_{2}+\vec{S}_{3}-\frac{SH\vec{e}_{z}}{3J_{1}}\right)^{2}\right.\\ &\left.+\frac{6S^{2}J_{2}}{J_{1}}-3S^{2}-\frac{S^{2}H^{2}}{9J_{1}^{2}}\right],\end{split} (S5)

NpN_{p} is the number of triangular plaquettes. We can immediately see that, under the assumption NUC=3{N_{\text{UC}}}=3, any state with

S→1+S→2+S→3=S​H​e→z3​J1\vec{S}_{1}+\vec{S}_{2}+\vec{S}_{3}=\frac{SH\vec{e}_{z}}{3J_{1}} (S6)

is a ground state, as long as this condition can be met, i.e., H≤9​J1H\leq 9J_{1}. For H>9​J1H>9J_{1}, the ground state is given by the fully polarized state with S→i=S​e→z\vec{S}_{i}=S\vec{e}_{z}. The ground state energy per site is given by

Egs,clN={3​J2−3​J12−H218​J1H≤9​J1,3​J1+3​J2−HH>9​J1.\frac{E_{\text{gs,cl}}}{N}=\left\{\begin{array}[]{ll}3J_{2}-\frac{3J_{1}}{2}-\frac{H^{2}}{18J_{1}}&H\leq 9J_{1},\\ 3J_{1}+3J_{2}-H&H>9J_{1}.\end{array}\right. (S7)

The full ground state manifold is too large to be entirely investigated in this work, hence we will focus on four classical configurations shown in fig. S1. The angles are chosen such that the defining property Eq. (S6) is fulfilled.

S2.2 Four-Site Unit Cell

In the four-sublattice phase, the classical Hamiltonian may be rewritten as

ℋ=N​J4​S2​[(∑i=14S→i−S​H​e→z2​J)2−S2​(H2+16​J2)4​J2],\mathcal{H}=\frac{NJ}{4S^{2}}\left[\left(\sum_{i=1}^{4}\vec{S}_{i}-\frac{SH\vec{e}_{z}}{2J}\right)^{2}-\frac{S^{2}(H^{2}+16J^{2})}{4J^{2}}\right], (S8)

where J=J1+J2J=J_{1}+J_{2}. Similar to the tree-site unit cell, any configuration with ∑i=14S→i=S​H​e→z2​J\sum_{i=1}^{4}\vec{S}_{i}=\frac{SH\vec{e}_{z}}{2J} is a ground state, as long as H≤8​JH\leq 8J and the fully polarized state for H>8​JH>8J. Hence the ground state energy per site is given by

Egs,clN={−H2+16​J216​JH≤8​J,3​J−HH>8​J..\frac{E_{\text{gs,cl}}}{N}=\left\{\begin{array}[]{ll}-\frac{H^{2}+16J^{2}}{16J}&H\leq 8J,\\ 3J-H&H>8J.\end{array}\right.. (S9)

Again, the classical ground state manifold is massively degenerate. We here consider the four states shown in fig. S2.

Appendix S3 Expansion in S−1S^{-1}

S3.1 Outline

The main goal of our computation is to obtain the proper ground state within the framework of Holstein Primakoff, i.e., the ground state up to some order in S−1S^{-1}. There is one caviat: We cannot perform an exact computation at an arbitrary order in the expansion. However, we can treat all terms beyond S−1S^{-1} in a mean-field manner such that at most quadratic terms remain.

To obtain the ground state energy, we first need to plug in the Holstein Primakoff representation of the spins into the Hamiltonian and expand in S−1S^{-1}

ℋ(Θ)=∑n=02S−n/2ℋ(n)(Θ)+∑n=3∞S−n/2ℋ¯(n)(Θ),\mathcal{H}(\Theta)=\sum_{n=0}^{2}S^{-n/2}\mathcal{H}^{(n)}(\Theta)+\sum_{n=3}^{\infty}S^{-n/2}\overline{\mathcal{H}}^{(n)}(\Theta), (S10)

where an overline indicates treatment in mean-field theory until the Hamiltonian contribution is at most quadratic. The Hamiltonian in this case is a function of the set of classical angles Θ\Theta that we can, in principle, choose arbitrarily.

Now, two things are needed for the full self-consistent ground state: First, we need to know the renormalization of the angles such that all terms linear in a bosonic operator in Eq. (S10) vanish. Second, we need to evaluate the ground state energy given a certain set of angles.

S3.2 Angle Renormalization

The angle renormalization is straightforward. We choose an initial configuration Θ(0)\Theta^{(0)} defined by

ℋ(1)​(Θ(0))=0,\mathcal{H}^{(1)}(\Theta^{(0)})=0, (S11)

which is the same as requiring Θ(0)\Theta^{(0)} is a classical ground state configuration. The renormalized angles

Θ[2​n]=∑m=0nΘ(2​m)Sm\Theta^{[2n]}=\sum_{m=0}^{n}\frac{\Theta^{(2m)}}{S^{m}} (S12)

are determined by requiring

ℋ(1)​(Θ[2​n])+∑m=1nℋ¯(2​m+1)​(Θ[2​n])Sm=0+𝒪⁡(S−n−1).\mathcal{H}^{(1)}(\Theta^{[2n]})+\sum_{m=1}^{n}\frac{\overline{\mathcal{H}}^{(2m+1)}(\Theta^{[2n]})}{S^{m}}=0+\mathcal{O}(S^{-n-1}). (S13)

Our goal is to obtain the ground state energy up do 𝒪⁡(S−2)\mathcal{O}(S^{-2}), hence Θ(4)\Theta^{(4)} can only enter through the classical energy contribution. However since Θ(0)\Theta^{(0)} is a classical ground state configuration, Θ(4)\Theta^{(4)} is irrelevant for our purposes as linear deformations in the angles lead to at least quadratic deformations in the classical energy. Hence for our purposes, the equation

ℋ(1)​(Θ[2])+ℋ¯(3)​(Θ[2])S=0+𝒪⁡(S−2).\mathcal{H}^{(1)}(\Theta^{[2]})+\frac{\overline{\mathcal{H}}^{(3)}(\Theta^{[2]})}{S}=0+\mathcal{O}(S^{-2}). (S14)

is sufficient to obtain the renormalized angles.

S3.3 Quantum Ground State Energy

S3.3.1 Matrix Representation of the Hamiltonian

With the angles being properly renormalized, we are left only with quadratic bosonic terms from Eq. (S10), i.e. we can readily write down the Hamiltonian up to order 𝒪⁡(S−3)\mathcal{O}(S^{-3})

ℋ⁡(Θ)=ℋ(0)​(Θ[2])+1S​ℋ(2)​(Θ[2])+1S2​ℋ¯(4)​(Θ[0])+𝒪⁡(S−3).\begin{split}\mathcal{H}(\Theta)=&\mathcal{H}^{(0)}(\Theta^{[2]})+\frac{1}{S}\mathcal{H}^{(2)}(\Theta^{[2]})\\ &+\frac{1}{S^{2}}\overline{\mathcal{H}}^{(4)}(\Theta^{[0]})+\mathcal{O}(S^{-3}).\end{split} (S15)

Note that the above expansion is not the only possible expansion up to this order. In fact, it might seem unintuitive to not expand every term explicitly, e.g.

ℋ(0)​(Θ[2])=ℋ(0)​(Θ(0))+(Θ(2)⋅∇)2ℋ(0)(Θ(0))2​S2.\mathcal{H}^{(0)}(\Theta^{[2]})=\mathcal{H}^{(0)}(\Theta^{(0)})+\frac{(\Theta^{(2)}\cdot\nabla)^{2}\mathcal{H}^{(0)}(\Theta^{(0)})}{2S^{2}}. (S16)

The reason for keeping the expansion the way of Eq. (S15) is that it is numerically much more stable. The key lies in the fact that an expansion like

cos⁡(ϕ+δ​ϕ)=cos⁡(ϕ)−δ​ϕ​sin⁡(ϕ)+𝒪⁡(δ​ϕ2)\cos(\phi+\delta\phi)=\cos(\phi)-\delta\phi\sin(\phi)+\mathcal{O}(\delta\phi^{2}) (S17)

disrupts the boundedness of the cosine, cos⁡(ϕ+δ​ϕ)∈[−1,1]\cos(\phi+\delta\phi)\in[-1,1] while cos⁡(ϕ)−δ​ϕ​sin⁡(ϕ)∈(−∞,∞)\cos(\phi)-\delta\phi\sin(\phi)\in(-\infty,\infty). Physically, this is reasonable, as an expansion like Eq. (S16) could lead to Heisenberg interactions to be renormalized beyond the spectrum of the operator.

Let us now turn in more detail to the treatment of the different terms in Eq. (S15). ℋ(0)​(Θ[2])=N​Ecl​(Θ[2])\mathcal{H}^{(0)}(\Theta^{[2]})=NE_{\text{cl}}(\Theta^{[2]}) is simply the classical energy evaluated at the renormalized angles, while ℋ(2)\mathcal{H}^{(2)} and ℋ¯(4)\overline{\mathcal{H}}^{(4)} are the first and second order quantum corrections. The former contains only terms quadratic in ai,ai†a_{i},a_{i}^{\dagger} while the latter includes quadratic contributions as well as constants from the mean-field decoupling.

We may rewrite ℋ(2)\mathcal{H}^{(2)} and ℋ¯(4)\overline{\mathcal{H}}^{(4)} by transforming to momentum space and using

a𝐤=(a1,𝐤,…,aNUC,𝐤,a1,−𝐤†,…,aNUC,−𝐤†)T.a_{\mathbf{k}}=(a_{1,\mathbf{k}},\dots,a_{{N_{\text{UC}}},\mathbf{k}},a_{1,-\mathbf{k}}^{\dagger},\dots,a_{{N_{\text{UC}}},-\mathbf{k}}^{\dagger})^{\text{T}}. (S18)

This leads to an expression of the form

ℋ(2)+1S​ℋ¯(4)=12​∑𝐤a𝐤†​M𝐤​a𝐤−Δ𝐤\mathcal{H}^{(2)}+\frac{1}{S}\overline{\mathcal{H}}^{(4)}=\frac{1}{2}\sum_{\mathbf{k}}a_{\mathbf{k}}^{\dagger}M_{\mathbf{k}}a_{\mathbf{k}}-\Delta_{\mathbf{k}} (S19)

where we drop the arguments from now on and assume the renormalized angle is used to the appropriate order. In Eq. (S19), M𝐤M_{\mathbf{k}} is a matrix of the form

M𝐤=(A𝐤B𝐤B−𝐤∗A−𝐤∗)=(A𝐤B𝐤B𝐤A𝐤),M_{\mathbf{k}}=\left(\begin{array}[]{cc}A_{\mathbf{k}}&B_{\mathbf{k}}\\ B_{-\mathbf{k}}^{\ast}&A_{-\mathbf{k}}^{\ast}\end{array}\right)=\left(\begin{array}[]{cc}A_{\mathbf{k}}&B_{\mathbf{k}}\\ B_{\mathbf{k}}&A_{\mathbf{k}}\end{array}\right), (S20)

with A𝐤A_{\mathbf{k}} determined form ai,𝐤†​aj,𝐤a_{i,\mathbf{k}}^{\dagger}a_{j,\mathbf{k}} terms and B𝐤B_{\mathbf{k}} from ai,𝐤†​aj,𝐤†a_{i,\mathbf{k}}^{\dagger}a_{j,\mathbf{k}}^{\dagger} terms. Δ𝐤\Delta_{\mathbf{k}} is the vacuum energy. At order S−1S^{-1}, Δ𝐤=tr⁡(A𝐤)\Delta_{\mathbf{k}}=\tr{A_\vk}, stemming from the fact that the bottom right A𝐤A_{\mathbf{k}} matrix in Eq. (S20) creates non-normal ordered terms ai,−𝐤​aj,−𝐤†a_{i,-\mathbf{k}}a_{j,-\mathbf{k}}^{\dagger}. At order S−2S^{-2}, Δ𝐤\Delta_{\mathbf{k}} also contains all terms from the mean-field contractions. Note furthermore that we assumed

A−𝐤∗=A𝐤,B−𝐤∗=B𝐤.A_{-\mathbf{k}}^{\ast}=A_{\mathbf{k}},\quad B_{-\mathbf{k}}^{\ast}=B_{\mathbf{k}}. (S21)

For coplanar configurations, this is true at order 𝒪⁡(S−1)\mathcal{O}(S^{-1}) as there is a residual S​O​(2)SO(2) symmetry in the definition of Eq. (S4) related to the choice of plane. We can use this freedom to keep Sy=S′yS^{y}=S^{\prime y}, such that there are only real coefficients in front of any operator in the expansion in position space. This implies that any imaginary contribution in the matrix Eq. (S20) originates from the connections ei​𝐤⋅𝐝e^{i\mathbf{k} \cdot\mathbf{d}} from transformation to momentum space. We will later show that this leads to the statement being true at order 𝒪⁡(S−2)\mathcal{O}(S^{-2}).

To diagonalize the Hamiltonian, we will perform a Bogoliubov transform. That is, we introduce matrices T𝐤T_{\mathbf{k}} and

Y=(𝟏NUC00−𝟏NUC),Y=\left(\begin{array}[]{cc}\mathbf{1}_{N_{\text{UC}}}&0\\ 0&-\mathbf{1}_{N_{\text{UC}}}\end{array}\right), (S22)

Y​M𝐤​T𝐤​e→i=T𝐤​T𝐤−1​Y​M𝐤​T𝐤​e→i=±ωi,𝐤​T𝐤​e→i,YM_{\mathbf{k}}T_{\mathbf{k}}\vec{e}_{i}=T_{\mathbf{k}}T_{\mathbf{k}}^{-1}YM_{\mathbf{k}}T_{\mathbf{k}}\vec{e}_{i}=\pm\omega_{i,\mathbf{k}}T_{\mathbf{k}}\vec{e}_{i}, (S27)

The condition of symplecticity translates to the normalization

vi,𝐤†​Y​vi,𝐤=±1.v_{i,\mathbf{k}}^{\dagger}Yv_{i,\mathbf{k}}=\pm 1. (S28)

Let us quickly prove that the expectation values in Eqs. (S32-S35) are real. To do so, we assume that Eq. (S20) holds for the matrix that we diagonalize. Then by reality of ω𝐤\omega_{\mathbf{k}}

T𝐤†​M𝐤​T𝐤=T𝐤T​M𝐤∗​T𝐤∗=T𝐤T​M−𝐤​T𝐤∗,T_{\mathbf{k}}^{\dagger}M_{\mathbf{k}}T_{\mathbf{k}}=T_{\mathbf{k}}^{T}M_{\mathbf{k}}^{\ast}T_{\mathbf{k}}^{\ast}=T_{\mathbf{k}}^{T}M_{-\mathbf{k}}T_{\mathbf{k}}^{\ast}, (S37)

we know that T−𝐤=T𝐤∗T_{-\mathbf{k}}=T_{\mathbf{k}}^{\ast}. As clearly (γ𝐤(i​j))∗=γ−𝐤(i​j)(\gamma_{\mathbf{k}}^{(ij)})^{\ast}=\gamma_{-\mathbf{k}}^{(ij)}, for the MF-expectation values

mi​j∗=1N∑𝐤γ𝐤(ij)∗(V𝐤V𝐤†)j​i∗=1N∑𝐤γ−𝐤(i​j)(V−𝐤V−𝐤†)j​i.m_{ij}^{\ast}=\frac{1}{N}\sum_{\mathbf{k}}\gamma_{\mathbf{k}}^{(ij)\ast}(V_{\mathbf{k}}V_{\mathbf{k}}^{\dagger})_{ji}^{\ast}=\frac{1}{N}\sum_{\mathbf{k}}\gamma_{-\mathbf{k}}^{(ij)}(V_{-\mathbf{k}}V_{-\mathbf{k}}^{\dagger})_{ji}. (S38)

Using the fact that the sum is symmetric around 𝐤=0\mathbf{k}=0, we thus know that mi​j∗=mi​jm_{ij}^{\ast}=m_{ij} and similarly ni,δi,Δi​j∈ℝn_{i},\delta_{i},\Delta_{ij}\in\mathbb{R}, hence the statement of Eq. (S21) remains true at order S−2S^{-2}.

Appendix S4 Ground State Algorithm

Lastly, let us describe the algorithm used to obtaining the proper, self-consistent ground state. That is, we want to determine the state at wich the mean-field expectation values computed from the diagonalization of the matrix M𝐤M_{\mathbf{k}} are identical to the values plugged in.

Formally, this is possible analytically though not feasible. We will thus restrict ourselves to a finite lattice with PBC and approximate the self-consistent solution. Since some regions are classically unstable, we have two choices left, which will be discussed in the following subsections. For both, we normalize J1=1J_{1}=1.

S4.1 Local Algorithm

The local algorithm works at a single point in parameter space J2,HJ_{2},H at a given finite, periodic lattice.

  1. 1.

    Diagonalize M𝐤M_{\mathbf{k}} at order S−1S^{-1} at all allowed 𝐤\mathbf{k}.

  2. 2.

    Compute ground state energy corrections and mean-field expectatino values FF.

  3. 3.

    Define new mean-field expectation values Fnew=sin2⁡(θ)​FF_{\text{new}}=\sin^{2}(\theta)F.

  4. 4.

    Diagonalize M𝐤M_{\mathbf{k}} for all 𝐤\mathbf{k} and compute energy and mean-field expectation values FF.

  5. 5.

    Define new mean-field expectation values by a mixing angle Fnew=sin2⁡(θ)​Fold+cos2⁡(θ)​FF_{\text{new}}=\sin^{2}(\theta)F_{\text{old}}+\cos^{2}(\theta)F.

  6. 6.

    Repeat from step 4 until energy has converged or maximum amount of recursions is reached.

As a convergence condition, we assume a Cauchy-sequence like criterion, i.e., if for the last ten recursions, |δ​Ei−δ​Ej|≤10−9​∀i,j\absolutevalue{\delta E_i-\delta E_j}\leq 10^{-9}\forall i,j.

S4.2 Stable Algorithm

Since some configurations are classically unstable but may be stabilized by quantum corrections, we may also use a different algorithm.

First, the initial mean-field expectation values and energy is evaluated at a known stable point, J2,i,HiJ_{2,\text{i}},H_{\text{i}} using the local algorithm. Then, along a chosen path in parameter space J2​(t),H​(t)J_{2}(t),H(t) to the final parameters J2,f,HfJ_{2,\text{f}},H_{\text{f}} at a given step size Δ​J2,ΔH\Delta J_{2},\Delta_{H}. At each step, the previous set of mean-field parameters is used as input, and the new set of parameters is evaluated until the final point is reached. At this point, step 4 to 6 of the local algorithm are performed.

Note that there is one caveat to each of the algorithms, resolved by the respective other. The local algorithm may become unstable due to a classical instability despite there being a self-consistent solution, while the stable algorithm may reside in a state that is not the ground state.

Appendix S7 Transition to the fully polarized phase

Here we derive the transition magnetic field between the fully polarized phase and the V phase for the J1−J2−hJ_{1}-J_{2}-h model. This transition can be computed exactly using the global spin conservation. The spin-12\frac{1}{2} Hamiltonian is defined as

H=H0−h​∑iSiz≡J1​∑⟨i​j⟩𝐒i⋅𝐒j+J2​∑⟨⟨i​k⟩⟩𝐒i⋅𝐒k−h​∑iSizH=H_{0}-h\sum_{i}S_{i}^{z}\equiv J_{1}\sum_{\expectationvalue{ij}}\mathbf{S}_{i}\cdot\mathbf{S}_{j}+J_{2}\sum_{\expectationvalue{\expval{ik}}}\mathbf{S}_{i}\cdot\mathbf{S}_{k}-h\sum_{i}S_{i}^{z} (S103)

where the double braket denotes next-nearest neighbor bonds. Again the Hamiltonian conserves StotzS_{\rm tot}^{z} thus we can apply the trick in the previous section. The critical field for polarization is the lowest magnetic field at which the system becomes fully saturated in magnetization, i.e. Stotz=N/2=L2/2S^{z}_{\rm tot}=N/2=L^{2}/2. For this to happen, the Stotz=N/2−1S^{z}_{\rm tot}=N/2-1 sector must have lower energy than the sector with Stotz=N/2S_{\rm tot}^{z}=N/2, thus the critical field hch_{c} satisfies

E0​(N2)−hc×N2=E0​(N2−1)−hc×(N2−1)E_{0}(\frac{N}{2})-h_{c}\times\frac{N}{2}=E_{0}(\frac{N}{2}-1)-h_{c}\times(\frac{N}{2}-1) (S104)

where E0​(N)E_{0}(N) is a short notation for the energy in the Stotz=NS^{z}_{\rm tot}=N sector without magnetic field (of H0H_{0}). Note that the Stotz=N/2S_{\rm tot}^{z}=N/2 sector has only one state, with all spins pointing along Sz=12S^{z}=\frac{1}{2}, and the total energy is given by

E0​(N/2)=H0​|Stotz=N2⟩=3​N​J1​14+3​N​J2​14=34​N​(J1+J2)E_{0}(N/2)=H_{0}\ket*{S_{\rm tot}^z = \frac{N}{2}}=3NJ_{1}\frac{1}{4}+3NJ_{2}\frac{1}{4}=\frac{3}{4}N(J_{1}+J_{2}) (S105)

since there are three bonds per site. While the sector with Stotz=N/2−1S_{\rm tot}^{z}=N/2-1 has exactly NN states, each of which has N/2−1N/2-1 spins pointing in Sz=12S^{z}=\frac{1}{2} and one spin pointing in Sz=−12S^{z}=-\frac{1}{2}. Next we need to find the lowest energy in this sector, let us denote the state with Snz=−12S_{n}^{z}=-\frac{1}{2} by |fn⟩\ket{f_n}, and consider the energy function of such a state.

J1∑i,j∈{a1,a2,a3}[Siz​Sjz+12​(Si+​Sj−+Si−​Sj+)]​|fn⟩=J12​∑δ|fn±δ⟩+(3​N4−3)​J1​|fn⟩\begin{split}J_{1}&\sum_{i,j\in\{a_{1},a_{2},a_{3}\}}\left[S_{i}^{z}S_{j}^{z}+\frac{1}{2}\left(S_{i}^{+}S_{j}^{-}+S_{i}^{-}S_{j}^{+}\right)\right]\ket{f_n}=\frac{J_{1}}{2}\sum_{\delta}\ket{f_{n\pm\delta}}+(\frac{3N}{4}-3)J_{1}\ket{f_n}\end{split} (S106)

with δ∈{a1,a2,a3}\delta\in\{a_{1},a_{2},a_{3}\} and a3=a2−a1a_{3}=a_{2}-a_{1}. Now consider the polarizing transition at J2=0J_{2}=0 only, thus we consider

HJ1​|fn⟩=J1​(3​N4−3)​|fn⟩+J12​∑δ|fn±δ⟩H_{J_{1}}\ket{f_n}=J_{1}\left(\frac{3N}{4}-3\right)\ket{f_n}+\frac{J_{1}}{2}\sum_{\delta}\ket{f_{n \pm\delta}} (S107)

Fourier Transform gives

E0​(N2−1)​|fk⟩=J1​[(3​N4−3)+∑δcos⁡(k.δ)]E_{0}(\frac{N}{2}-1)\ket{f_k}=J_{1}\left[\left(\frac{3N}{4}-3\right)+\sum_{\delta}\cos(k.\delta)\right] (S108)

hence, using a1=(12,3/2)a_{1}=(\frac{1}{2},\sqrt{3}/2) and a2=(1,0)a_{2}=(1,0), the lowest energy is

min⁡[E0​(N/2−1)]=J1​(3​N4−4.5){\rm min}[E_{0}(N/2-1)]=J_{1}\left(\frac{3N}{4}-4.5\right) (S109)

hence

hc​(J2=0)=4.5h_{c}(J_{2}=0)=4.5 (S110)

This number is veried by DMRG with an error <10−2<10^{-2}.

Next let us consider the generic case for J2≠0J_{2}\neq 0. The ground state energy in the two sectors is the same as J2=0J_{2}=0 case except for a change in the momentum space distribution of the energies. The total energy in the N/2−1N/2-1 sector is thus

E0​(N2−1)=(1+J2/J1)​(3​N4−3)+∑δcos⁡(k.δ)+(J2/J1)​∑ηcos⁡(k.η)E_{0}(\frac{N}{2}-1)=(1+J_{2}/J_{1})\left(\frac{3N}{4}-3\right)+\sum_{\delta}\cos(k.\delta)+(J_{2}/J_{1})\sum_{\eta}\cos(k.\eta) (S111)

where η\eta are the three next-nearest-neighbor vectors, and we set J2J_{2} in units of J1J_{1}. Hence

min⁡[E0​(N2−1)]=(1+J2/J1)​(3​N4−3)+min⁡[∑δcos⁡(k.δ)+J2J1​∑ηcos⁡(k.η)]{\rm min}[E_{0}(\frac{N}{2}-1)]=(1+J_{2}/J_{1})\left(\frac{3N}{4}-3\right)+{\rm min}\left[\sum_{\delta}\cos(k.\delta)+\frac{J_{2}}{J_{1}}\sum_{\eta}\cos(k.\eta)\right] (S112)

This minimum can be readily found for different J2/J1J_{2}/J_{1}. The resultant hch_{c} is a piecewise function:

hc​(J2/J1)={4.50<J2/J1≤184​(1+J2/J1)J2/J1>18h_{c}(J_{2}/J_{1})=\begin{cases}4.5&0<J_{2}/J_{1}\leq\frac{1}{8}\\ 4(1+J_{2}/J_{1})&J_{2}/J_{1}>\frac{1}{8}\end{cases} (S113)

where the piece-wise function has a kink exactly at J2/J1=18J_{2}/J_{1}=\frac{1}{8} where the Dirac QSL is present at zero field.
